s.d: to say goodbye
s.g: to bid goodbye to; to take leave of

s.d: to employ certain set phrases as a part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
s.c: It is possible that in some contexts ἀσπάζομαι could be interpreted as ‘to visit,’ so that in ⟦Acts 18:22|Acts 18:22⟧ one may render ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν as ‘visiting the church’ rather than as ‘greeting the church.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: to be happy about something, on the basis that it would prove particularly welcome (thus implying a type of future orientation)
s.g: to be happy about; to anticipate with pleasure
s.c: In order to render the future implications of ἀσπάζομαι in ⟦Hebrews 11:13|Hebrews 11:13⟧, one may be able to translate ‘and looked forward with happiness to what was going to happen.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in ⟦Hebrews 11:13|Hebrews 11:13⟧, see ἀσπάζομαι LN 34.55.

s.d: to welcome something or someone, with focus upon the initial greeting
s.c: In some languages, however, it may be difficult to speak of ‘welcoming promises,’ but one can often render this relationship as ‘they were happy to know about what had been promised.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in ⟦Hebrews 11:13|Hebrews 11:13⟧, see ἀσπάζομαι LN 25.130.

s.d: to say goodbye
s.g: to bid goodbye to; to take leave of

s.d: (derivative of ῥάπτω ‘to sew together,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to being without a seam, that is, without being sewn together
s.c: In some languages it may be necessary to describe such a seamless robe as ‘his robe was woven as just one piece of cloth.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
s.d: to cause someone to be pleased with someone or something
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to cause someone to be pleased with something’ is expressed as ‘to cause someone to be happy about’ or ‘to cause someone to feel good about.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
s.d: pertaining to that which pleases someone
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘this pleased the Jews’ is ‘this caused the Jews to be happy’ or even ‘this caused the Jews to say, That’s fine.’

s.d: pertaining to being proper or right, with the implication of desirable

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a king of Nabatean Arabia

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Goodness
s.d: the quality of moral excellence
s.c: It is possible, however, that ἀρετή in ⟦2 Peter 1:3|2 Peter 1:3⟧ denotes the manifestation of (divine) power (see LN 76.14).

s.d: a manifestation of power characterized by excellence
s.g: wonderful act; powerful deed; wonderful deed

s.d: young of sheep ({L:πρόβατον<SDBG:πρόβατον>}); often used for ritual sacrifice
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between male and female lambs. It is therefore essential in any figurative reference to male persons to employ an appropriate term for lamb. In a number of languages, of course, a lamb is simply referred to as a ‘young sheep’ or ‘child sheep.’|Perhaps the most widespread story about cultural differences in Bible translation is the one which refers to the translation of ‘lamb’ as ‘little seal of God’ in an Eskimo language. However, there is no evidence that this type of rendering was ever used, since in matters of appearance, habitat, and behavior, lambs and little seals have practically nothing in common. Furthermore, Eskimo languages have terms for ‘lamb’ and in some instances, at least, use the expression ‘young, woolly goat,’ since wild goats are well known and wool is well known as an imported product.

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀριθμός<SDBG:ἀριθμός:000000>}[a] ‘number,’ {D:60.1}) to employ numbers in determining a quantity{N:001}
any cardinal number
s.c: It may be important to add a marginal note to ⟦Revelation 13:18|Revelation 13:18⟧ to indicate that the number 666 was actually derived from adding up the numerical values of the letters of a name.

s.d: the sum or total of a numbered quantity

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Judea

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a companion of Paul

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
s.g: to eat a meal; to have a meal
s.c: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to eat the earlier meal of the day
s.c: Some scholars, however, interpret ἀριστάω in ⟦John 21:12|John 21:12⟧ as meaning any kind of meal (see ἀριστάω, LN 23.20), and therefore one would translate as ‘Jesus said to them, Come have something to eat’ or ‘… have a meal.’|In a number of languages the earlier meal of the day may be spoken of as ‘the morning meal’ or ‘the first meal.’ In some languages it is actually called ‘the leftovers meal,’ but see the discussion on meals at different times of the day at LN 23.25.

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › Left, Right, Straight Ahead, Opposite
s.d: pertaining to being to the left of some point of reference
s.c: In ⟦2 Corinthians 6:7|2 Corinthians 6:7⟧ the phrase ὅπλον ἀριστερόν, literally ‘left-hand weapon,’ refers to a weapon used by the left hand and therefore a defensive weapon, while ὅπλον δεξιόν, literally ‘weapon for the right hand,’ refers to an offensive weapon.|For an interpretation of ἀριστερός as part of an idiom in ⟦Mark 10:37|Mark 10:37⟧, see LN 87.35.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.c: The left hand is designated in a number of languages by an idiomatic phrase which normally contrasts with expressions for the right hand. For example, one may often speak of the left hand as ‘the bad hand’ or ‘the weak hand,’ and in some instances as ‘the anus hand,’ since this is the hand used in cleansing the body after defecation. See also LN 8.32.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person whose family is greeted in the Epistle to the Romans

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of ἄριστον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of {L:ἄριστον<SDBG:ἄριστον:000001>}[b], {D:23.23})
s.g: a meal; a banquet; a feast
s.c: Though ἄριστον, δεῖπνον, and βρῶσις are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of ⟦Mark 6:21|Mark 6:21⟧ that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a less important meal, normally in the earlier or middle part of the day
pertaining to what is sufficient for some purpose and accordingly resulting in satisfaction{N:001}
to be sufficient or adequate for a particular purpose, with the implication of leading to satisfaction
s.g: to be sufficient; to be adequate; to be enough

s.d: to be happy or content as the result of having what one desires or needs to be
s.g: to be content; to be satisfied
s.c: In a number of languages ‘to be content’ is expressed negatively, for example, ‘to not complain.’ In other instances, one may be forced to employ a type of direct or indirect discourse, for example, ‘to acknowledge that it is enough’ or ‘to say, It is all that is needed.’

s.d: large wild four-footed mammal with thick fur and doglike face; walks on all fours but may stand up on its back legs to get a better view; may be 2 m. tall when standing up and weigh over 200 kilos; feeds on roots, berries, wild fruit, mice, and lizards, and, occasionally, small livestock; Ursus arctos syriacus; dangerous when provoked or robbed of cubs; associated with violence and danger
s.c: The term ἄρκος ‘bear’ occurs in the NT only in ⟦Revelation 13:2|Revelation 13:2⟧ as a description of the apocalyptic beast. In languages where a term for bear is not known, it is probably best to borrow a word and describe the referent in a footnote or glossary. In ⟦Revelation 13:2|Revelation 13:2⟧ a somewhat descriptive phrase is sometimes employed, for example, ‘with large feet having claws like those of an animal called bear.’ By this means the information about the bear’s feet has been incorporated into the text, but usually it is better to leave such information to a marginal note.

s.d: open vehicle with two or four wheels; harnessed to and pulled by horses; used in war or for travelling
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 9:9|Revelation 9:9⟧ the reference is to war chariots drawn by horses, while in ⟦Acts 8:28|Acts 8:28⟧, ⟦Acts 8:38|Acts 8:38⟧ the reference is to a travelling chariot in which the Ethiopian official was riding. In languages which have no technical term for chariot, it is possible to speak of a war chariot as ‘a war carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn cart for fighting.’ A travelling chariot may be described as ‘a travelling carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn vehicle.’ A further description of such chariots may be given in a glossary.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a cryptic place name designating the territory which will be the scene of the final battle of the forces of good and evil
to promise a person for marriage
s.g: to be engaged; to be promised in marriage
s.c: It may be important to note in the margin of a text that in biblical times the act of betrothal was regarded as binding, so that the breaking of a betrothal was legally equivalent to divorce.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: a part of the body which joins two parts together
s.c: In the use of ἁρμός the emphasis is not upon the joints as a moving part of the body but as a means by which different parts of the body are effectively joined together. Accordingly, ἁρμός overlaps in meaning with ἁφή (LN 18.17). For problems in translating ⟦Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12⟧, see LN 8.62.

s.d: to say that one does not know about or is in any way related to a person or event{N:001}
s.c: In translating ἀρνέομαι and ἀπαρνέομαι, one can often use an equivalent phrase such as ‘to say that one does not know’ or ‘to say that one has nothing to do with.’|In denying an event, as in ⟦Luke 8:45|Luke 8:45⟧, it may be possible to translate ‘but they all said they knew nothing about it.’ It is also possible to deny having done something, and therefore one may translate the response in ⟦Luke 8:45|Luke 8:45⟧ as ‘but they all said that they did not do it’ or ‘… that they did not touch him.’

s.dp: Association › Establish or Confirm a Relation
s.d: to deny any relationship of association with someone
s.c: In a number of languages one may best translate ‘deny’ as ‘to make manifest not to know.’ Accordingly, one may translate the first part of ⟦Luke 12:9|Luke 12:9⟧ as ‘whoever shows people that he does not know me’ or ‘whoever refuses to admit that he does know me.’ Denial need not involve some verbal formulation, though in some languages this is the most common practice. See also LN 33.277.

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Agree, Consent
s.d: to refuse to agree or consent to something
s.g: to refuse to agree to; to not consent to

s.dp: Think › To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately
s.d: to refuse to give thought to or express concern for{N:002}
s.g: to disregard; to pay no attention to; to say no to
s.c: There are a number of problems involved in rendering appropriately ἀρνέομαι and ἀπαρνέομαι as in ⟦Luke 9:23|Luke 9:23⟧ and ⟦Mark 8:34|Mark 8:34⟧.|In a number of languages it simply makes no sense to translate ‘to say No to oneself,’ nor is it possible in many instances to use an expression such as ‘to deny oneself,’ since it almost always implies to deny oneself something. Sometimes the meaning may be expressed in a figurative or idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to refuse to pay attention to what one’s own desires are saying’ or ‘to refuse to think about what one just wants for oneself.’ In certain instances other kinds of idioms may be employed, for example, ‘to put oneself at the end of the line’ or even ‘to say to one’s heart, Keep quiet.’

s.dp: Guide, Discipline, Follow › Follow, Be a Disciple
s.d: to refuse to follow someone as a leader
s.g: to refuse to follow; to refuse to obey; to reject

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hypocrisy, Pretense
s.d: to behave in a way which is untrue to one’s real self, in a sense of denying certain valid aspects of one’s personality
s.g: to be false to oneself; to be untrue to oneself
s.c: It is possible in some languages to translate ‘he cannot be false to himself’ in ⟦2 Timothy 2:13|2 Timothy 2:13⟧ as ‘he cannot be different from what he really is’ or ‘he cannot be otherwise than good.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀρήν<SDBG:ἀρήν:000000>} ‘lamb,’ {D:4.24}) young of sheep ({L:πρόβατον<SDBG:πρόβατον:000000>}); often used for ritual sacrifice; or a sheep of any age
s.c: In the one context in the NT, namely, ⟦Revelation 13:11|Revelation 13:11⟧, in which ἀρνίον refers literally to a sheep, it is used in a phrase referring to the horns of an ἀρνίον. In such a context the reference is undoubtedly to a ‘ram,’ that is to say, the adult male of sheep.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀρνίον<SDBG:ἀρνίον:000000>}[a] ‘lamb,’ {D:4.25}) a follower of Christ, with the implication of helplessness and dependence
s.g: a person who is like a lamb
s.c: Compare LN 11.30 and LN 11.31.

s.d: a title for Christ
s.c: ἀρνίον as a title of Jesus Christ occurs only in the book of Revelation, but it is used there more than twenty times. In contrast with ἀρνίον in βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου ‘feed my lambs’ (⟦John 21:15|John 21:15⟧; see LN 11.29), designating people who need care and help, the supplementary components of meaning in ἀρνίον involve the atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross. Some persons have wanted to eliminate the notion of ‘lamb’ in this title, especially in the case of languages in which sheep are looked down on as relatively worthless scavengers (as is the case in certain tropical areas of the world), but in view of the significance of the symbolism of ‘lamb’ in terms of OT sacrificial practices, it is wrong to avoid a term meaning ‘lamb.’ A marginal note, however, may be necessary to explain the significance of this title.

s.d: to plow, as a means of preparing land for sowing
s.g: to plow; to use a plow
s.c: In biblical times plows did not turn over the soil but were used simply to break the surface, seldom to a depth of more than about ten inches (or twenty five centimeters).

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry
s.d: a flat triangular blade (the “plowshare”) made of hard wood or metal, connected to a handle; used to cut the soil in preparation for the sowing of seed or the planting of seedlings
s.c: In most parts of the world at least some type of plow is known, and in ancient Palestine the plow was not a turning plow, but one which simply dug a relatively shallow furrow, but in doing so, loosened the soil. Where plows are not known or used, it is possible to employ a descriptive phrase such as ‘a tool for preparing the ground for sowing.’ For ἄροτρον as part of a Semitic idiom in ⟦Luke 9:62|Luke 9:62⟧, see LN 68.6.

s.d: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
s.g: to rob; to carry off; to plunder; to forcefully seize

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἁρπαγή<SDBG:ἁρπαγή:000000>}[a] ‘act of plunder,’ {D:57.235}) that which is taken by force or plundered
a state of strong desire to gain things and, if necessary, by violent means
to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
s.g: to rob; to carry off; to plunder; to forcefully seize
s.c: This interpretation of ⟦Philippians 2:6|Philippians 2:6⟧ reflects the position of Jesus after the incarnation and the fact that he had no thought of trying to become equal with God because he already possessed all of the qualities of deity. Some traditional translations have rendered the latter part of ⟦Philippians 2:6|Philippians 2:6⟧ as ‘did not think it robbery to be equal with God,’ but see LN 57.236.

s.d: that which is to be held on to forcibly
s.g: something to hold by force; something to be forcibly retained
s.c: Compare the rendering of ἁρπαγμός in LN 57.235. Since ἁρπαγμός may mean not only ‘to grasp something forcefully which one does not have’ (LN 57.235) but also ‘to retain by force what one possesses,’ it is possible to translate ⟦Philippians 2:6|Philippians 2:6⟧ in two quite different ways. This second interpretation of ἁρπαγμός presumes the position of Jesus prior to the incarnation and hence his willingness to experience the kenosis or ‘emptying’ of his divine prerogatives. In any translation of ⟦Philippians 2:6|Philippians 2:6⟧ it is important that both possible renderings be clearly indicated, one in the text and the other in the margin.

s.d: to grab or seize by force, with the purpose of removing and/or controlling
s.g: to seize; to snatch away; to take away
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 13:19|Matthew 13:19⟧ the context as a whole is figurative, but a more or less literal rendering of ‘snatches’ or ‘seizes’ is probably satisfactory.

s.d: to attack, with the implication of seizing
s.c: It is also possible that in ⟦Matthew 11:12|Matthew 11:12⟧ ἁρπάζω is to be understood in the sense of ‘attack’: βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν ‘violent men attack it.’

s.d: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
s.g: to rob; to carry off; to plunder; to forcefully seize

s.d: to gain control over by force
s.g: to gain control over; to seize; to snatch away
s.c: Though in ⟦John 10:28|John 10:28⟧ ἁρπάζω would appear to be in a literal context in view of the expression ἐκ τῆς χειρός μου ‘out of my hand,’ nevertheless ἁρπάζω is certainly figurative in meaning and so is χείρ ‘hand.’

s.d: (derivative of ἁρπάζω[a] ‘to carry off by force,’ {D:57.235}) one who carries off the possessions of another by force
s.c: For an interpretation of ἅρπαξ as an adjective in ⟦Luke 18:11|Luke 18:11⟧, see LN 25.25.

s.d: pertaining to being destructively vicious
pertaining to being violently greedy
s.c: In ⟦Luke 18:11|Luke 18:11⟧ ἅρπαξ may also be interpreted as a noun (see LN 57.239).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Pay, Price, Cost
s.d: the first or initial payment of money or assets, as a guarantee for the completion of a transaction or pledge (in the NT ἀρραβών is used only figuratively in referring to the Holy Spirit as the pledge or guarantee of the blessings promised by God){N:001}
pertaining to what cannot or must not be spoken

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: to be sick or ill, as a state of powerlessness

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sexual Misbehavior
s.d: a male partner in homosexual intercourse
s.c: It is possible that ἀρσενοκοίτης in certain contexts refers to the active male partner in homosexual intercourse in contrast with μαλακός, the passive male partner (LN 88.281).

s.d: the male of any living creature

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Involving Successive Generations
s.d: (an idiom, literally: male that opens the womb, and closely related in meaning to {L:πρωτότοκος<SDBG:πρωτότοκος:000000>}[a], ‘firstborn,’ {D:10.43}) the first male offspring of a female
s.c: A literal translation of the idiom ‘male that opens the womb’ may be extremely misleading in some languages, since it may refer to the first act of sexual intercourse and not to the birth of the first, male child.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a friend of Paul

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Greek goddess worshiped especially in Asia Minor

s.dp: Artifacts › Boats and Parts of Boats
s.d: a cloth attached above a boat in such a way as to catch the wind and thus propel the boat through the water
s.c: In ⟦Acts 27:40|Acts 27:40⟧ (the only occurrence of ἀρτέμων in the NT) the reference may be to the foresail, that is, a relatively small sail toward the prow of the ship. A sail may be described in some languages as ‘a piece of cloth to make the ship move’ or ‘cloth on the ship to catch the wind.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event (in a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items)

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
s.d: (an idiom, literally: the present hour) an emphatic reference to a point of time which is simultaneous with another point of time
s.g: at this very moment; at this very time

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Birth, Procreation
s.d: pertaining to having been born recently
s.c: ‘Newly born babies’ may be rendered as ‘babies who have just been born’ or ‘babies who have just begun to live.’

s.d: pertaining to being qualified to perform some function
a relatively small and generally round loaf of bread (considerably smaller than present-day typical loaves of bread and thus more like rolls or buns)
any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
s.c: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as ⟦Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11⟧ as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
s.g: bread offered to God; consecrated bread
s.c: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
s.g: to eat a meal; to have a meal
s.c: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ ⟦Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7⟧. No doubt the reference in ⟦Acts 20:7|Acts 20:7⟧ is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See LN 23.28.

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Earn, Gain, Do Business
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to eat one’s own bread) to earn a living by one’s own efforts
s.g: to earn a living; to earn a livelihood

s.d: to add condiments to food
s.c: In rendering ⟦Luke 14:34|Luke 14:34⟧ it may be necessary to translate ἀρτυθήσεται as ‘to cause it to taste like salt again’ or ‘to cause it to taste right again.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Beings
s.d: a chief or highly important angel
s.c: An archangel may be described as ‘one who commands other angels’ or ‘a leading angel’ or ‘a chief angel.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: pertaining to having existed for a long time in the past, with the possible implication of such existence from the beginning of an event or state
s.g: for a long time; from the beginning; ancient

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the son of Herod I
initiation of an action, process, or state of being
s.c: It would also be possible to treat ἀρχή in ⟦Mark 1:1|Mark 1:1⟧ as indicating sequence (Domain 61), so that the contents of verse 1 could be regarded as a type of title for the following section. It seems far better, however, to regard ἀρχή in ⟦Mark 1:1|Mark 1:1⟧ as being closely related to what immediately follows in verse 2, so that one may translate ‘the good news about Jesus Christ the Son of God began as the prophet Isaiah had written …’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
s.d: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
one who or that which constitutes an initial cause
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἀρχή in ⟦Revelation 3:14|Revelation 3:14⟧ as meaning ‘ruler’ (see LN 37.56).

s.d: the sphere of one’s authority or rule
s.g: sphere of authority; limit of one’s rule

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἄρχω<SDBG:ἄρχω:000000>} ‘to rule,’ {D:37.54}) one who rules or governs

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
s.g: power; authority; lordship; ruler; wicked force
s.c: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of ⟦Ephesians 1:21|Ephesians 1:21⟧ some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. For example, Ephesians 2:2 is rendered in some languages as ‘at that time you lived in the way in which the spirit that governs this world dictated you should live. This is the way the one who rules over the power in space commanded you to live. This is the very spirit that now commands the people who disobey God.’

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Basic Principles or Features Defining the Nature of Something
s.d: elementary and preliminary aspects defining the nature of something
s.c: Compare also the occurrence of ἀρχή in ⟦Hebrews 5:12|Hebrews 5:12⟧ in which it serves to reinforce the meaning of στοιχεῖα (see LN 58.19).

s.d: the corner of a two-dimensional object, such as a sheet of cloth
one who causes something to begin
s.c: For another interpretation of ἀρχηγός in ⟦Hebrews 2:10|Hebrews 2:10⟧, see ἀρχηγός LN 36.6.

s.d: a person who as originator or founder of a movement continues as the leader
s.c: In order to indicate clearly the significance of ἀρχηγός in ⟦Hebrews 2:10|Hebrews 2:10⟧, it may be important to employ a translation such as ‘who established a way of salvation and leads people to it.’ But it is also possible to understand ἀρχηγός in ⟦Hebrews 2:10|Hebrews 2:10⟧ as meaning only the ‘initiator’ or ‘founder’ (see ἀρχηγός LN 68.2).

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀρχιερεύς<SDBG:ἀρχιερεύς:000001>}[b] ‘high priest,’ {D:53.89}) pertaining to the high priest
a principal priest, in view of belonging to one of the high-priestly families
s.c: In a number of languages ‘chief priests’ are referred to simply as ‘big priests’ or ‘important priests.’

s.d: the principal member among the chief priests
the head shepherd who directs the activities of other shepherds (in its only NT occurrence; a figurative reference to Christ)

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Christian in Colossae
one who is the head of and who directs the affairs of a synagogue
s.g: president of a synagogue; leader of a synagogue

s.d: one who is a master or expert builder
chief tax collector, in the sense of one who controlled activities of certain other tax collectors
s.g: chief tax collector; director of tax collectors
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἀρχιτελώνης as meaning a principal or important tax collector rather than one who controlled the activities of other tax collectors.

s.d: the head servant in charge of all those who served at meals or feasts
s.c: It is also possible that ἀρχιτρίκλινος in ⟦John 2:8|John 2:8⟧ refers to the master of ceremonies or the toastmaster at the feast.

s.d: to rule or govern, with the implication of preeminent position and status
to initiate an action, process, or state of being
s.c: ἄρχω may also be used in an absolute sense in which the related activity is merely implied: αὐτὸς ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ‘when Jesus began, he was about thirty years old’ ⟦Luke 3:23|Luke 3:23⟧. In rendering ⟦Luke 3:23|Luke 3:23⟧, it may be useful to translate as ‘when Jesus began his ministry, he was about thirty years old.’

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
s.d: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
s.c: It is also possible to understand this expression in ⟦Acts 1:22|Acts 1:22⟧ as ‘beginning from the time of John’s baptizing (him).’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἄρχω<SDBG:ἄρχω:000000>} ‘to rule,’ {D:37.54}) one who rules or governs

s.dp: Courts and Legal Procedures › Judge, Condemn, Acquit
s.d: a minor government official serving as a judge
s.c: Though in ⟦Luke 12:58|Luke 12:58⟧ ἄρχων has essentially the same reference as κριτής and δικαστής (LN 56.28), the meaning differs in that ἄρχων represents government authority functioning in judgment on cases.

s.dp: Supernatural Beings and Powers › Supernatural Powers
s.d: (ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος - title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
s.g: power; authority; lordship; ruler; wicked force
s.c: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of ⟦Ephesians 1:21|Ephesians 1:21⟧ some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

s.d: (a title, literally: ruler of the Jews) a member of the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews{N:001}
an aromatic resin of a lily-like plant, often used for embalming a corpse
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ἄρωμα is ‘sweet-smelling herbs’ or ‘good-smelling leaves’ or ‘perfumed oil.’

s.d: pertaining to that which cannot be moved
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀσάλευτος<SDBG:ἀσάλευτος:000000>}[a] ‘immovable,’ {D:15.4}) pertaining to occurring in an unchangeable state
s.c: In a number of languages it may be better to express the concept of ‘enduring’ as ‘not ending,’ and accordingly one might translate this phrase in ⟦Hebrews 12:28|Hebrews 12:28⟧ as ‘God’s ruling over us will never end.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to a fire that cannot be put out
s.c: It may be necessary in some languages to render ‘unquenchable’ by an active equivalent, for example, ‘a fire that no one can put out.’

s.d: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice
s.g: to live in an ungodly manner; godlessness

s.d: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice
s.g: to live in an ungodly manner; godlessness

s.d: pertaining to living without regard for religious belief or practice

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sexual Misbehavior
s.d: behavior completely lacking in moral restraint, usually with the implication of sexual licentiousness
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ‘licentious behavior’ would be ‘to live like a dog’ or ‘to act like a goat’ or ‘to be a rooster,’ in each instance pertaining to promiscuous sexual behavior.

s.dp: Status › Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]
s.d: pertaining to being obscure or insignificant, with the possible implication of lacking in noble descent
s.c: In a number of languages, however, it would be important to avoid the double negative in ⟦Acts 21:39|Acts 21:39⟧ (despite the effectiveness of the litotes in Greek) by translating ‘a citizen of an important city.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
a state of incapacity to do or experience something
s.c: A literal rendering of this expression in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:9|2 Corinthians 12:9⟧ may not be meaningful, and in fact can be quite misleading. δύναμις is best interpreted as ‘God’s power’ and ἀσθένεια as the weakness which Paul experienced. Therefore, one may be able to translate as ‘my power is greatest when you are weak’ (see Today’s English Version).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: the state of being ill and thus incapacitated in some manner
s.c: It may be extremely difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking illness’ or ‘carrying away diseases.’ A strictly literal rendering of such an expression might suggest immediately that Jesus was a type of medicine man who healed others by taking upon himself precisely the same kinds of diseases (a widespread shamanistic practice). It may therefore be necessary in some languages to translate ⟦Matthew 8:17|Matthew 8:17⟧ as ‘he caused us to no longer have illness and disease.’ In this way, one may avoid a specific type of shamanistic practice which would be inappropriate in this context.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀσθένεια<SDBG:ἀσθένεια:000000>}[a] ‘weakness,’ {D:74.23}) a state of timidity resulting from a lack of confidence
to be in a state of incapacity or weakness
s.g: to be weak; to be unable to; to be limited in
s.c: In some languages it may be better to translate this expression in ⟦Romans 14:1|Romans 14:1⟧ as ‘welcome those who have only a little faith.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: to be sick and, as a result, in a state of weakness and incapacity
s.g: to be sick; to be ill; to be disabled

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀσθενέω<SDBG:ἀσθενέω:000000>}[a] ‘to be weak,’ {D:74.26}) an instance of weakness or limited capacity
s.c: In some languages it may be appropriate to translate τὰ ἀσθενήματα as ‘times when they are weak.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:ἀσθένεια<SDBG:ἀσθένεια:000000>}[a] ‘weakness,’ {D:74.23}) pertaining to a state of limited capacity to do or be something

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: pertaining to being morally weak and hence incapable of doing good
s.c: It is also possible to understand ἀσθενής in ⟦Romans 5:6|Romans 5:6⟧ as a helpless condition rather than moral weakness (see ἀσθενής LN 22.3).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: pertaining to being ill and, as a result, weak and incapacitated

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Trouble, Hardship, Distress
s.d: pertaining to a state of helplessness in view of circumstances
s.c: The meaning of ‘helpless’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘when we could not do anything about it.’ For another interpretation of ἀσθενής in ⟦Romans 5:6|Romans 5:6⟧, see ἀσθενής LN 88.117.

s.d: pertaining to being physically weak
s.c: Such a literal translation of this expression in ⟦1 Peter 3:7|1 Peter 3:7⟧, however, may be misleading, for in general τῷ γυναικείῳ is interpreted as a reference to one’s wife. Therefore, one may translate as ‘treating with respect one’s wife as the physically weaker partner’ or ‘… as of the weaker sex.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the Roman province of Asia, primarily the western part of present-day Turkey

s.d: (derivative of {L:Ἀσία<SDBG:Ἀσία:000000>} ‘Asia,’ {D:93.415}) a person who is a native of Asia
a high-ranking official in Asia Minor (in an area which is now Turkey)

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
to engage in some activity, with both continuity and effort
s.g: to do one’s best; to endeavor

s.d: a bag made of skin or leather; used for temporarily storing and carrying wine
s.c: A number of translators have attempted to substitute ‘bottles’ for ‘wineskins,’ but this has not been satisfactory, since fermenting wine does not normally break glass bottles, while it would break old wineskins. In circumstances in which the use of wineskins is not known, it may be necessary to employ some type of descriptive phrase (for example, ‘a container made of skin’ or ‘a closed bag of skin’ or ‘a goat skin like a bottle’) and a fuller explanation in the margin.

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: pertaining to experiencing happiness, implying ready and willing acceptance

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: pertaining to not being wise
certain set phrases that are part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
pertaining to having no spot or stain

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Holy, Pure
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἄσπιλος<SDBG:ἄσπιλος:000000>}[a] ‘spotless, without stain,’ {D:79.59}) pertaining to being without that which might mar one’s moral character
kind of poisonous snake; associated with lurking danger
s.c: The terms ἀσπίς and ἔχιδνα may be used to refer to almost any kind of poisonous snake, and since at least some type of poisonous snake occurs in practically all parts of the world, there is usually little difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term. One can, however, always employ a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a snake whose bite causes death.’

s.d: pertaining to being unwilling to be reconciled to others
s.g: irreconcilable; unwilling to be at peace with others

s.d: a Roman copper coin worth 1/16 of a denarius
s.c: See LN 6.79.

s.dp: Spacial Positions › At, Beside, Near, Far
s.d: a position extremely close to another position
s.g: very near; as close as possible

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city of Mysia
to be without a permanent residence and thus engaged in travelling from one place to another
s.g: to be homeless; to wander from place to place; to be constantly going from place to place
s.c: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:11|1 Corinthians 4:11⟧, see LN 85.80.

s.d: to not have a place of residence
s.g: to be homeless; to be without residence
s.c: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:11|1 Corinthians 4:11⟧, see ἀστατέω LN 15.25.

s.d: pertaining to being beautiful or attractive in terms of being well-formed

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: a star or a planet
s.c: Since in ⟦Jude 1:13|Jude 1:13⟧ godless people are likened to ‘wandering stars’ or ‘planets,’ it may be best to introduce this expression by a simile, for example, ‘they are like wandering stars.’ In some languages there is a serious difficulty involved in translating ἀστὴρ πλανήτης as ‘planet,’ since the planets or their courses through the heavens are regarded as beneficial. In ⟦Jude 1:13|Jude 1:13⟧ the focal meaning is upon the heretical nature of these godless persons who do not keep on the right course. It may therefore be necessary to translate ἀστέρες πλανῆται in ⟦Jude 1:13|Jude 1:13⟧ as ‘stars that do not stay where they should stay’ or ‘… do not remain in their right places.’ See also LN 15.26.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: (an idiom, literally: morning star) a planet which is conspicuous in the morning sky (usually either Venus or Mars)
s.g: morning star; bright star in the morning sky
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 2:28|Revelation 2:28⟧ the singular pronoun αὐτῷ refers to any and all of the persons in Thyatira, and therefore it is usually best rendered as plural. A literal rendering of ⟦Revelation 2:28|Revelation 2:28⟧ may be confusing, since it would suggest that God would be handing over the morning star to persons in Thyatira. A more satisfactory rendering may be ‘I will cause the morning star to shine upon them’ or possibly ‘I will bring light into their hearts.’

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: pertaining to the tendency to change and waver in one’s views and attitudes

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Love, Affection, Compassion
s.d: pertaining to a lack of love or affection for close associates or family
s.g: without normal human affection; without love for others

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Change an Opinion Concerning Truth
s.d: to go astray as the result of departing from the truth
s.g: to abandon the truth; to lose one’s way

s.dp: Physical Events and States › Thunder and Lightning
s.d: the flash of lightning
s.c: Terms referring to thunder and lightning often have important taboo connotations. The specific terms for thunder and lightning may be avoided and figurative expressions employed in their place in order to avoid danger which might occur from being struck by lightning or frightened by a thunderstorm. One can, therefore, expect in some languages a number of different terms, and it is important to avoid expressions which might have wrong connotations.

s.d: shafts or beams of light radiating from a source
s.c: It is often better to render ἀστραπή as a type of qualifying adverb, for example, brightly.

s.d: to give off or to reflect a very bright light{N:001}
s.g: to glisten; to dazzle; to gleam; to flash

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: a star or a planet
s.c: In selecting a term for ‘star,’ it is important to avoid an expression which may relate to only one set of stars, that is to say, a particular constellation, since there may be connotations associated with such a constellation which can radically alter the intent of a particular passage. Some constellations, for example, may be regarded as kindly disposed toward mankind, while others may be regarded as hostile.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: a group of stars
s.c: Normally a constellation may be described as ‘a group of stars’ or ‘a family of stars’ or ‘stars that travel together’ or even ‘stars that live together.’ It is possible, however, to interpret the occurrence of ἄστρον in ⟦Acts 7:43|Acts 7:43⟧ as being a reference to a particular planet (namely, Saturn) rather than a constellation.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
